documents.title: Navigating Complexity: How Context Shapes Debugging Strategy Choices Among Expert Developers

assets.alt: Figure 1. Three-phase study workflow, shown as three banners stacked from top to bottom. Phase 0, literature synthesis: derive candidate debugging contexts and strategies. Phase 1, survey: collect a sample of currently challenging debugging scenarios and their frequencies. Phase 2, expert interviews: obtain detailed accounts of strategy choice and adaptation grounded in those scenario types. The adjacent text specifies 35 survey respondents and 16 expert interviewees.

Figure 2. Network summarizing commonly reported debugging strategy transitions from 16 expert web developers. It is a descriptive model, not a decision tree: context questions do not uniquely determine the next strategy, and a missing edge does not rule out a transition. Six green ellipses are numbered: 1, Forward-reasoning; 2, Error-message; 3, Hypothesis-test; 4, Backward-reasoning; 5, Simplification; and 6, External Strategy. Starting from whether a defect is observable, the diagram connects a non-observable defect through codebase complexity (l) to forward reasoning. For an observable defect, clear messages (a) lead toward error-message debugging, vague messages (b) toward hypothesis testing, and client-side versus other failures (c) toward simplification or hypothesis testing. Error-message debugging connects through access to the codebase (d) to backward reasoning. Hypothesis testing connects through debugger availability (e) to backward reasoning, or through reproducibility (f), familiarity (g), and search-space size (h) to simplification. Constrained production, compiled-binary, or ownership contexts (i) distinguish external strategies from simplification. User-specific failures (j) also connect hypothesis testing to external strategies. Sporadic behavior or infeasible traces (k) connect backward reasoning back to hypothesis testing; legacy or unmaintained code (n) connects to backward reasoning. Forward reasoning connects through familiarity (m) toward hypothesis testing when familiar or external strategies when unfamiliar, and through reproducibility and a narrowed search space (o) toward simplification. Simplification connects through unsafe or limited opportunities to simplify (q) toward external strategies. Context boxes are blue for codebase characteristics, tan for defect characteristics, and pale yellow for environmental, tooling, and organizational constraints. The printed legend labels both codebase and defect characteristics as Table IV; the body text identifies codebase characteristics in Table V. Arrow weight encodes breadth of participant support: thick solid lines, at least 7 participants; thin solid lines, 4 to 6; dashed lines, 3 or fewer. Thick routes emphasize complexity to forward reasoning, clear errors to error-message debugging, debugger availability to backward reasoning, familiarity to hypothesis testing, and a large search space to simplification. Dashed routes include reproducible, narrowed problems from forward reasoning to simplification, sporadic or infeasible traces from backward reasoning to hypothesis testing, and unsafe simplification to external strategies. Table VII gives the associated conditions, participant evidence, and quotations.

documents.title: CoCapture: Effectively Communicating UI Behaviors on Existing Websites by Demonstrating and Remixing

assets.alt: Figure 1: The workflow of CoCapture. There are four steps of using CoCapture to communicate new UI behavior mockups on an existing website. (Step 1) Users first capture existing interface behaviors (base scene) by interacting with the website (scrolling), and CoCapture will automatically capture the Document Object Model (DOM) changes. (Step 2) In CoCapture’s main panel, users can add new behaviors on top of the base scene by demonstration; that is, by directly manipulating any elements (e.g., drag and drop the red element in the replay and see immediate changes). (Step 3) Users can remix (post-edit, e.g., change duration) added behaviors to finalize the mockup. (Step 4) Users can refer to the DOM elements or added behaviors in the textual description using hypertext.

Figure 2: CoCapture’s main panel (after Step 1 in Fig. 1). To create an animation, a user first clicks on an existing DOM element (b1) (can select multiple by holding Shift key down) from the base scene (B). Once recording starts (A), the user can demonstrate the desired behaviors by changing the elements’ properties (C) or directly dragging them in the base scene. Once the recording is finished, the demonstration will be appended to the Animation List (D) with a set of meta operations, such as adjust start/end time, replay, and preview. The user can write their question (E) and refer to the animations or DOM elements in the scene by selecting portions of text and clicking the ‘Link to a Reference’ button. Text with references, or hypertext, is in blue with a click affordance displaying the relevant context (i.e., highlight elements (b1), replay animations (D)). The process of the animation (inbetweening) will also be displayed (F). The user can also filter the Animation List (D) to only display the animations related to the selected elements.

Figure 3: For each created animation, CoCapture provides information that prompts users about the actions they can take, including creating visual tags and replaying or previewing the animation. It also supports a set of operations to make the creation process easier and more accurate, including a range slider for time adjustment, as well as options for cloning, changing, or deleting an element.

Figure 4: There are three steps to create hypertext: (1) select portions of the text in the question description, (2) click “Link to a Reference,” and either (3.1) select an element in the scene or (3.2) check an animation. The hypertext will be highlighted afterwards.
Position and rotation icon: overlapping circles ending in a filled circle.
Font-size icon: small and large capital A letters.
Visibility icon: an open eye.

Figure 5: Screenshots of two of the user study tasks: the Reddit website (left column), and an SVG game (right column). The screenshots with a red border (a, c) are the existing UIs, whereas the green ones (b, d) are the desired UIs that the participants were asked to create and describe during the study. The tasks were designed with three goals: realistic, common, and complex. For the Reddit website task, the issue with the existing UI is that some of the DOM elements are not responsive to window resizing user input. For the SVG game task, participants need to add new game behaviors such that when the game character hits the block and the star shape element, the game scene will change dynamically and a new element (the cyan shield shown in the last image) will be added to the scene.

Figure 6. Box plots of time in seconds, control in coral and CoCapture treatment in cyan. For visual-reference creation, control median is about 110 seconds, with middle half roughly 65–200, while CoCapture median is about 325, with middle half roughly 280–475 and a long upper whisker near 760. For writing text, control median is about 350 seconds, with middle half roughly 315–380, versus CoCapture median about 95, with middle half roughly 60–145. Control has high outliers near 490 seconds for visual references and near 560 and 800 for text. Participants spent more time creating visual references and less time writing with CoCapture; the source reports both differences p<.0001.

documents.title: EdCode: Towards Personalized Support at Scale for Remote Assistance in CS Education

assets.alt: Fig. 1. A diagram shows the process of using EdCode to make a request, write a response, and integrate a response. (1) Students select a portion of their code and click the ‘Help’ button next to the selection to initialize a request. (2) Students attach a title, description, and tags to the request and send it to instructors. (3) Instructors can see the code base and other relevant information in their interface where they could write a contextualized response to the request. To make their answers more contextualized, instructors can (1) select a portion of the text in their natural language answer and the relevant code context; (2) click the ‘link’ button to create the references, which will highlight the relevant code (hypertext) when clicking the references in the text. Fig. 3. The code publicity feature. Instructors first click the ‘Show this code’ button to select a portion of the code in original request that is necessary to understand the question for other students. documents.title: A Hybrid Crowd-Machine Workflow for Program Synthesis

assets.alt: Fig. 1. Bashon allows users to create Bash commands from natural language. It uses a hybrid workflow that integrates crowd workers and an AI for program synthesis. In this example, the user types a command in natural language: “List files that are modified more than 30 days ago under the css directory” and Bashon proposes three Bash commands. The user can press ‘Run’ to execute any of the proposed commands

Fig. 2. System diagram: This diagram plots both the original Tellina (blue) and Bashon’s (green) workflow. In Tellina’s workflow, first, a natural language query (1) is sent to an automated entity extraction process (2) which outputs a list of entities, their associated types, and the entity extracted query template (3). Then, the neural network (4) translates the query and the extracted entities into a list of commands (5) that is sent back to the user (6). In Bashon’s workflow, the natural language queries first go through the original Tellina system, with automated entity extraction (1-5). The results from this are then evaluated by crowd workers (7). If they are incorrect (8), they then go to crowd workers for entity extraction (9). Commands resulting from this re-extraction process go back to crowd workers for a final validation step (7), and the results of this are sent back to the end users (10).

Figure 3. Pipeline compares automated Tellina and crowd components. For 50 queries, Tellina entity extraction has 29.00% precision and 22.64% accuracy; crowd extraction has 85.99% precision and 91.99% accuracy (both marked with three asterisks in the source). Extracted entities and templates feed translation, producing candidate commands. Tellina execution filters invalid results, with 60.3% accuracy. A query such as show only .pdf files and the divided file-system outputs then go to crowd validation, which has 77.04% accuracy and returns valid commands.

Fig. 4. User interface of entity extraction task. Crowd workers can add one entity at a time by typing the entity they recognize in the query to the text box (1), and then select the type from a drop down list (2).

documents.title: On-Demand Collaboration in Programming
Towards Providing On-Demand Expert Support for Software Developers

assets.alt: Figure 1. Setup for our hypothetical assistant study. Developer participants were asked to bring their own task to complete, and ask questions from our hypothetical assistant as if it could answer any support question needed. Participants were still allowed to use traditional online resources and augment them with the assistant as they saw fit. Context related to their programming task was collected at the beginning of each study, and audio of their questions was recorded during the session.

Figure 2. Setup for our human expert assistant study. In each trial, one “requester” participant (developer) was paired with one “helper” (expert, based on a pre-study skill assessment). Participants could chat via either text or voice, and requesters were able to share their screen with helpers as needed using Skype. The helper was tasked with assisting the requester reactively, meaning that they only responded to queries, and did not proactively propose solutions or approaches. This simulates a “best case” (repeated, non-multiplexed helper) on-demand model where human experts are not expected to be continuously available between end-user queries.

documents.title: Expresso: Building Responsive Interfaces with Keyframes

assets.alt: Figure 1 presents an illustration of four different keyframes created in Expresso for a sample web page. Each keyframe is a rectangle of a different shape and size, representing different viewport sizes. The four keyframes appear as though on an x-axis, sorted by viewport width, with the narrowest keyframe on the left and the widest keyframe on the right. There is a bi-directional arrow above the set of keyframes with the label 'viewport width', providing a label for the axis. The sample web page shown in the keyframes is adapted from the Mozilla website that we used during one of our study tasks. Each keyframe has the following items: 1) a blue background, 2) the orange FireFox logo, 3) the text 'The new Firefox' in white font, 4) the text 'With 2x the speed, built-in privacy protection and Mozilla behind it, the new Firefox is the better way to browse' in white font, 5) a green rectangle representing a button, with the text 'Download Firefox' on it in white font, and 6) an illustration of an open laptop with a Firefox browser shown. Note that the element and viewport widths mentioned below are not to scale; the keyframes are shrunk down for the figure. Moving from left to right, the keyframes can be described as follows: The leftmost keyframe is called k_0 and has a width of 722 pixels. The viewport width is narrow compared to its height, and represents the portrait-view viewport on a mobile device. In keyframe k_0, the whole web page has a blue background. The other elements on the page are all horizontally centered and stacked vertically. At the top is the Firefox logo which is medium-sized. Below that is the text 'The new Firefox' in a small font size. Below that is the text 'Fast for good.' in a large font size. Below that is the long line of text 'With 2x the speed, built-in privacy protection and Mozilla behind it, the new Firefox is the better way to browse' in a very small font size. Below that is the green 'Download Firefox' button. Below that is the laptop illustration which is of medium size and which is at the bottom of the page. Note that the laptop's x-position is 148 pixels. The next keyframe is called k_1 and has a width of 990 pixels. The viewport width is approximately the same as the viewport height. In keyframe k_1, the UI elements have the same arrangement as in k_0, with all elements horizontally centered and stacked vertically. All elements are the same size as in k_0. Since k_1's viewport is wider, there is more margin to the left and right of elements. Note that the laptop's x-position is 203 pixels. The next keyframe is called k_2 and has a width of 1000 pixels. The viewport width is wider than the viewport height. In k_2, the page has the same elements as in k_0 and k_1, but a vastly different layout and some elements are different sizes. k_2 has more of a 2-column layout. In k_2, the blue background only takes up the top half of the page (the lower half of the page is a placeholder gray). The Firefox logo is smaller and is on the far-left edge of the page. The 'The new Firefox' text is of medium font size and appear directly to the right of the Firefox logo. Below the 'The new Firefox' text appears the 'Fast for good' text of large font size. Below that is the long line of text 'With 2x the speed, built-in privacy protection and Mozilla behind it, the new Firefox is the better way to browse' in a very small font size. Below that is the green button with the text 'Download Firefox'. The text elements and the green button are left-aligned with each other. On the right side of the screen is the laptop, of large size, with equal margin on its left and right sides. Note that the laptop's x-position is 550 pixels. The next keyframe is called k_3 and has a width of 1200 pixels. The viewport width is much wider than the viewport height. In k_3, the UI elements have the same 2-column arrangement as in k_2. The only difference is that, with the wider page size, the laptop has more margin on its left and right sides. Note that the laptop's x-position is 650 pixels. As a summary of the layouts, keyframes k_0 and k_1 have all elements horizontally centered and stacked vertically. k_2 and k_3 have the Firefox logo and all text on the left side of the page, and the laptop on the right side of the page. Each keyframe has a colored-strip beneath it to help in explaining transitions between keyframes. k_0 has a light green strip, k_1 has a magenta strip, k_2 has a turquoise strip, and k_3 has a brown strip. Each strip also has a label of the laptop's x-position on it, as the transitions highlighted in this figure are those for the laptop x-position. There is a colored-strip between each pair of adjacent keyframes representing the transition type. The colored-strip between k_0 and k_1 is a left-to-right gradient of light green to magenta, indicating a smooth transition between k_0 and k_1. Similarly, the colored-strip between k_2 and k_3 is a left-to-right gradient, of turquoise to light brown, indicating a smooth transition between k_2 and k_3. The colored-strip between k_1 (magenta) and k_2 (turquoise) is a solid color of magent indicating a jump transition between k_1 and k_2. Specifically, the magenta color means that the range between k_1 and k_2, namely viewport sizes 991 to 999 pixels, should continue the behavior for the laptop x-position from the smaller viewports. This means that the laptop (and all UI elements) are shown horizontally centered and stacked vertically for the range of viewports 991 to 999 pixels wide. There are range arrows below the set of keyframes indicating the laptop x-position. For the range of viewports less than 1000 pixels wide, there is an arrow pointing left with the label 'laptop is centered in viewport' beneath it. For the range of viewports greater than or equal to 1000 pixels wide, there is an arrow pointing right with the label 'laptop is on the right side of the viewport'.

Figure 2 presents an illustration of the Expresso user interface. In this illustration, the sample web page used is meant to look like a shoe catalog on a shopping site, and is adapted from the Bass website. On the left side of the figure is part 'a', which is the web page viewing area. For this example, the viewing area contains the shoe catalog website, containing the following elements: 1) a brown rectangle at the top representing the page header, with the 'Bass' logo centered, 2) on the left side, a list of menu items with text 'WEEJUNS', 'WOMEN', 'MEN', 'KIDS', 3) a tall and thin brown rectangle representing the border of the left menu bar, 4) in the body of the web page, six Bass loafer shoes arranged in 2 rows of 3; from left to right, the top row contains light green, red, and yellow shoes; from left to right, the bottom row contains pink, lilac, and brown shoes, 5) the pink shoe is currently in 'selected' mode, where it has a black border around it. At the bottom of the figure is part 'b', which is the keyframe menu. It contains a list of keyframes for the current responsive web page, represented in a list from left to right with 'width' and 'height' viewport sizes. For this particular example, the keyframe sizes are, from left to right, 1) width 635 pixels and height 752 pixels, 2) width 769 pixels and height 752 pixels, 3) width 780 pixels and height 752 pixels, and 4) width 1200 pixels and height 752 pixels. Currently the keyframe of width 780 pixels is selected, which is indicated by its tab having a blue background; the web page shown in the viewing area in the illustration is this keyframe of width 780 pixels. To the right of the keyframe list, the bottom part of the figure also has a button with the label 'Result webpage (click to resize)' which users can click in order to enter 'resize' mode. To the right of this are 'Create new keyframe' and 'Delete current keyframe' buttons. On the right side of the figure is part 'c', which is the element property values menu. This menu appears in the format of a table and contains the current property and transition values for the currently selected UI element in the viewing area, in this case, the pink shoe. Each option has a radio button next to it, and the user has selected the "V Guerrero, S Perez, J Abreu, R Devers, ..." option as the best option, and can next click the "Select" button to lock it in. For the "statistic" parameter, the parameter values after the user has selected the best suggestion are "Home Runs", "Hits", "Doubles", "Triples", "Batting Average", "Walks", "Stolen Bases", "Caught Stealing", "Strikeouts".

An illustration of ParamMacros’s execution interface and the Major League Baseball (MLB) statistics website. It shows an interactive interface for the question "How many <statistic> did <player> have?", with the parameter as dropdown menus -- the "statistic" dropdown with value set to "Hits" and the "player" dropdown with value set to "R Devers". The result of running the macro for these values is 165, which is highlighted in a simplified illustration of the Major League Baseball website that is shown (it's a table with first column Players plus playing position, second column Hits ("H" for short), third column doubles ("2B" for short), fourth column triples ("3B" for short), and fifth column home runs ("HR" for short)). Therefore each row is the data for a given player. The third row has data for Rafael Devers, and the "Hits" value for Rafael Devers's row is 165, so this is the answer to the parameterized question for the current parameter values.

A program description we would present to a user who has created demonstrations for the question "For the player who had the <most/least> <stat1>, what was their <stat2>?". The first part of the description is the general logic stemming from the user's original demonstration; the first step is a "click" which is influenced by the "stat1" parameter. The second step is a "print" where the entry (e.g., row) is determined by looking for the superlative (most/least parameter) value over the stat1 parameter. The printed column is then determined by attribute stat2. This is the logic the inference algorithm has inferred based on the user's first demonstration, which it has greedily subbed in parameters as much as possible. If the user doesn't want the program logic to depend on parameters in some cases, and instead just on the concrete values from the demonstration, they can make these corrections through the interface, which offers these concrete values as alternatives (e.g., the user can switch the value of the suplerative from the radio button value "stat1" to the other value presented, "Doubles", which was the example value used in the demonstration for "stat1"; similarly they can switch the printed attribute from "stat2" to "Batting Average"). The second part of the program description describes the behavior inferred from this second demonstration. Again the first step is a "click" which is influenced by the "stat1" parameter. The second step is a "print" where the entry (e.g., row) is determined by looking for the superlative (most/least parameter) value over the stat1 parameter. This is the logic that will be run specifically for "stat2" equals "Position".

An imaginary website titled "The Food Store" (for the purposes of explaining our inference algorithm). The left side of the page has the subheading "FRUITS", with 4 rows of fruits. Each row contains an illustration of the fruit, then to its right the name of the fruit, then to its right the price of the fruit. Specifically the fruits are: Apple (90 cents), Banana (25 cents), Pineapple (2 dollars), Fig (one dollar). The right side of the page has parallel information for veggies (e.g., Broccoli, Carrot). The illustration also highlights certain parts of the page and their XPaths. A red dotted rectangle around the 4 rows of fruits represents the common prefix XPath that each fruit text has: html > ... > .section > .fruit. Then each fruit row has a purple dotted rectangle around it, representing the next part of the XPath string, div[i], where "i" is the row index. This figure illustrates the process of generalizing a parameter XPath from the unique XPath string for original value "Apple" to a generalized XPath formula to match all values for the "fruit" parameter. The first line of the figure is the unique XPath "html > ... > .section[1] > .fruit[1] > div[1] > span[2]", which matches the text "Apple" only. assets.alt: Fig. 1. An illustration of ScrapeViz’s final state after the user has completed the IMDb scraping task in section IV. ScrapeViz gives users a programming by demonstration (PBD) authoring interface and interactive storyboard-like visual representations of their web scraping macro. A user begins with a single website viewport (D) and provides demonstrations (C and A for movie titles, K and M for actor names, S for birthdate) of the scraping and navigation actions they want to perform – ScrapeViz adds colored borders to indicate selected elements, opens new viewports for website pages navigated to, and generalizes these actions across UI elements and pages (using the PBD algorithm described below). assets.alt: Figure 1: (A) The proposed digital assistant, Adasa, identifies user’s questions or commands regarding ADAS features in human language and responds with answers or actions accordingly. (B) Adasa is integrated into a commercially available vehicle for evaluation and a real-world driving user study. (C) Adasa is able to access vehicle CAN signals via Bluetooth to conduct system diagnosis or system control. (D) Adasa setup, driver enables Adasa by pressing the button on the wheel to start the conversation.

Figure 2: Overview of Adasa system, which is designed based on recent publications [20] and integrated with a commercially available vehicle [8]. Driver’s voice captured by the microphone is translated into its text equivalent ( 1 ) and is passed to Query Classifier to identify the type of query ( 2 ). Execution Logic operates the query ( 3 ) and retrieves the information needed from either Knowledge Base ( 4 ) or the vehicle ( 5 ) depends on the type of query. Vehicle-data Ingestor receives the CAN data through the vehicle interface and records the status of each signal in Vehicle State Repository ( 6 - 7 ). Once the result is passed back to Execution Logic ( 8 ), the response is converted to a WAV file and output to the speaker to answer driver’s questions ( 9 - 10 ).

documents.title: Arboretum and Arbility: Improving Web Accessibility Through a Shared Browsing Architecture

assets.alt: Figure 1 depicts a blind end user using Arbility to interact with a browser-based calendar for placing an online order. The blind end user communicates with a sighted crowd worker via the Arbility chat panel, while the crowd worker's interface shows a mirrored version of the blind end user's calendar. A large computer mouse cursor indicates the crowd worker's click event on a specific calendar date. This click event is sent back to the blind end user, visualized as an arrow extending from the cursor back to the Arbility interface. The blind end user accepts the proposed click event, visualized by an arrow from their current calendar view to an updated calendar page state.

Figure 2 shows an excerpt from a chat log between the end user and remote crowd worker. The crowd worker says, "Want me to select a time too?" and the end user replies with "3pm." The crowd worker then proposes the click action on 3pm, which appears in the chat log as "CrowdWorker wants to click 3:00 PM." Beneath this message, there are four options available to the end user: Accept, Reject, Focus, and Request Label.

This illustration shows a simple node and edge tree representing a part of a website's DOM. Each node is a turquoise circle with a letter in it. The root of the tree is at the top of the illustration. Child nodes appear below parent nodes. The root node is A and has 2 children: node B, on the left, and node C, on the right. Node B has child node D. Node C has child node E. Parent-child relationships are shown by black single-direction arrows, drawn from the parent node to the child node. This particular tree represents the initial state of the DOM for the example in this paper section. The next illustration shows a later state of the DOM.

This illustration shows a simple node and edge tree representing a part of a website's DOM. Each node is a yellow circle with a letter in it. The root of the tree is at the top of the illustration. Child nodes appear below parent nodes. This particular tree represents the same part of the website as in the previous illustration, but instead at a later point in time when the user visits the website. The website DOM has changed. Now root node A has 3 children: node Y on the left, node B in the middle, and node C on the right. Node B has child node X below it. Nodes Y and C have no children. In summary, compared to the previous illustration, the changes are: 1) Node A has a new child (node Y), 2) node B's child changed from node D to node X, and 3) node C no longer has any children (previously it had child node E). Parent-child relationships are shown by black single-direction arrows, drawn from the parent node to the child node.

Figure 3 is a complex system diagram depicting the interface between the Arbility tool and the Arboretum architecture. The Arbility tool consists of a chat interface (A) and a Chromium web browser (B). The Arboretum architecture consists of a web server (C) and a mirroring module (D). The blind end user interacts with the Arbility chat interface by inputting messages, which are sent to the Arboretum web server and forwarded to sighted crowd workers. These crowd workers then send proposed actions and events back to the Arboretum server, which forwards them to the end user for acceptance or rejection. If the end user accepts the events, the corresponding page updates are executed in the Arbility Chromium browser, which then sends these changes to the Arboretum mirroring module. The mirroring module then syncs these changes with the Arboretum web server so that the updates due to the accepted action are also visible to remote crowd workers. The diagram depicts these components and their interactions as labeled boxes with directed arrows between them.

This illustration shows the Needleman-Wunsch sequence alignment Arbility computes between the two versions of the DOM tree, seen in the previous illustrations in this paper section. In this illustration, there is a top row of turquoise circles corresponding to the tree from the first illustration. From left to right, the nodes are: A, B, D, C, E. There is a bottom row of yellow circles corresponding to the tree from the second illustration. From left to right, the nodes are: A, Y, B, X, C. Note that the order of nodes presented here is the depth-first search pre-order traversal. For nodes that appear in both rows, a black line connects them to indicate they are matched in the sequence alignment algorithm. Here, the connected nodes are: row 1's A and row 2's A; row 1's B and row 2's B; and row 1's C and row 2's C. Nodes that were not matched are faded out.

Figure 4 depicts each of the three task pages and their corresponding task question and reason for inaccessible content. The task question for the Calorie Counter page is "How many calories are needed to lose 1 pound?" and this content is inaccessible because it encodes this information in a visual canvas element. The task question for the Gary Turk Video page is "Name the person who did sound engineering for the video" and this content is inaccessible because it requires a mousedown event to reveal, whereas screen reader interactions typically simulate click events. The task question for the Noodlehead Menu page is "Name one $8 noodle dis that is indicated as spicy" and is inaccessible because spiciness is indicated only by red text CSS styling.

Figure 5 is a two-part table with quantitative results for each of the three tasks. The first part of the table shows the accuracy by study participant group. Blind (solo) participants achieved accuracies of 0, 63, and 14 on the Counter, Video and Menu tasks respectively. Sighted (solo) participants achieved accuracies of 100, 90, and 86 on the Counter, Video, and Menu tasks respectively. Blind (solo) participant times were n/a, 108, and 133 on the Counter, Video, and Menu tasks respectively. (Note: the time for completion on the Counter task was not applicable because no blind participant successfully completed this task.) Sighted (solo) participant times were 62, 93, and 82 on the Counter, Video, and Menu tasks respectively. Blind plus Sighted (Arbility) participant times were 418, 240, and 304 on the Counter, Video, and Menu tasks respectively.

assets.alt: Figure 1: The code on the right produces the interface on the left. Here, asynchronous calls are made to the Facebook API using the fb_request function to fetch a list of friends (line 1) and a profile picture for each friend (lines 2—5). These values are placed into the friends and pics constraint variables respectively. Lines 9—21 declare a template that depends on these variables. As the list of friends is loading, friends.state will be pending, so the message “Loading friends…” is displayed (line 10). After the list of friends has loaded (lines 12—20) the picture for each friend is displayed alongside their name. While the application is waiting for the Facebook API to return a picture URL for a friend, a loading image (loading.gif) is displayed (line 15). The code also correctly notifies the user of any errors (lines 11, 17).
Figure 2: An illustration of a jQuery UI slider widget. Constraint variables can be attached to track the value of this widget.

Figure 3: A color selector that uses constraint variables to automatically update the preview color and hex value text. A constraint variable tracks the values for each of the red, green, and blue sliders (r, g, and b respectively.) A fourth constraint variable (hex) computes a hex color value. Finally, constraints update the background color and text of the color selector to reflect the slider values.
Figure 4: (Left) An illustration of an interactive behavior where hovering over one block highlights the other block. (Right) the FSM used by both blocks to track their state.

Figure 5: The FSM of asynchronous constraints in ConstraintJS. Asynchronous constraints are constraints that don’t have a value until after some delay period, e.g. data returned from network or file system queries. While the constraint is waiting for a value, the FSM is in the “Pending” state. When it successfully receives a value, it enters the “Resolved” state. If there is an error or the request times out, it enters the “Rejected” state.

Figure 6: An illustration of Bubble Cursors [6]. Clickable “targets” are light grey-filled circles. When the cursor is too far from any of the targets, a grey dotted halo appears around the cursor (A). When a target is in range (B), the halo becomes red and shrinks enough that it intersects the target, which turns dark grey. The ConstraintJS implementation of this application allows all of this behavior to be expressed declaratively.

Figure 7: A scatterplot application implemented with ConstraintJS. By default, constraints set the position of every data point to reflect the values of an underlying data model (A). When a point is dragged (B), a constraint in the opposite direction updates the underlying data model based on the position of the point, which in turn, is constrained to the mouse’s position. The axes may also be dragged (C) and constraints automatically update the axis labels to reflect its position. Finally, axes’ scales may be changed (D) by dragging a point while holding SHIFT. This example illustrates how one-way constraints in ConstraintJS may be combined with FSMs to enable functionality that was previously only possible with multi-way constraints.

Figure 8: An illustration of a touchscreen-based application written with ConstraintJS. Constraints control the position, scale, and angle of photos, which users can manipulate with one or two fingers. When two fingers touch a photo, a red slider appears that controls the photo’s opacity and can be changed using a third finger. Constraints set the position and text of the slider.

assets.alt: Fig. 1. chat.codes is a communication tool for programmers that combines a shared editor (left) with synchronous text chat (right). Users can click on any given message to see the state of the code when that message was sent (A). chat.codes also allows programmers to see when code was edited by displaying edit messages in-line with chat messages (B). These messages can be expanded to reveal a full diff (Figure 5 shows what clicking the ‘(more)’ button displays). Users can also easily “point” to regions of code through a simple highlighting interaction (as Figure 3 illustrates).

Fig. 2. chat.codes is implemented as a website and as a plugin for the Atom IDE. Atom users can use chat.codes in their IDE, which will automatically converts their editor into a shared editor. Programmers can click a button to create a unique shareable URL that helpers can then visit. Helpers can then access the requester’s IDE over the web by visiting that URL.

Fig. 3. chat.codes enables programmers to point to regions of code in their messages through a Markdown-based syntax. Users can also easily specify what region of code they want to refer to by simply highlighting that region in the code window, which automatically inserts an appropriate code pointer.

Figure 4. Four states for creating code pointers in chat. From state 1, with no chat text selected, selecting code inserts and selects a complete pointer (state 2); clearing the code selection removes it. While the full pointer is selected, changing the code selection updates its target. From state 3, with ordinary chat text selected, selecting code turns that text into a pointer (state 4). While pointer label text is selected, changing the code selection changes the target while preserving the label; clearing code selection removes the pointer and leaves the text selected.

Fig. 5. In chat.codes, code edit summaries are displayed inline with chat messages. By default these summaries only indicate which user changed which files. They can also be expanded to reveal a full diff, as shown above.

documents.title: EDBooks: AI-Enhanced Interactive Narratives for Programming Education

assets.alt: Fig. 1. An illustration of EDBook content that describes the basics of Python modules. Readers learn through an interactive dialog (left column) that includes a natural language didactic dialog, multiple choice questions, and code writing questions. With EDBook, readers work through this narrative over time. At any point in the narrative, they can also interact with a context-aware LLM for additional questions. These dialogs can also include larger code samples that are incrementally built and explained over the course of the narrative (right column). Deictic pointers (represented as blue lines) can link the narratives with specific parts of code. At the bottom of the leftmost column, the reader is given three options for how to proceed with the narrative: two pre-built questions (“is random a built-in module?” and “Could we call import inside of rollDice?”) and the option to query an LLM.

A continuum runs from less constrained to more constrained dialog. From left to right: open-ended LLMs such as ChatGPT; topic-shifting agents; pre-written tree- or state-based dialogs; and pre-written linear dialogs. EDBooks is positioned above the tree- or state-based category.

Fig. 3. Conceptually, EDBook dialogs are trees (left) but these trees are visually simplified and flattened in the reader UI (right) for readability. On the left is an illustration of an example dialog tree. Each node in the tree represents a message and is labeled according to its depth (1–5) and breadth-first search order (a–z). For example, 3a represents the leftmost node in the third layer. EDBook allows instructors to define a ‘target’ node (message 5d in this example) that represents completion of the learning goals for the page. In this example, the user is currently focused on message 4b, so ‘ancestor’ cells 1a, 2a, 3a, and 4b are visible in the UI (right). In the UI, users can also select pre-existing subsequent messages (5b and 5c) or write a custom message (‘Edit’) that will query an LLM to add a response message. The user’s current node is part of the dialog tree but not on the path of the target, 5d. Thus, the user is also nudged to go to a node that would move them back towards target node 5d by back-tracking to node 3b (with a “back to main thread” button). The UI also shows icons ( ) to indicate messages with multiple possible responses (right) and calls attention to the first message where the user’s path diverges away from the target message (in red ).
Fig. 4. Warning labels are added to any cells that contain unverified LLM-generated content.
Fig. 5. Instructors can work with larger codebases that change over time. Readers can see these incremental code edits, as diffs.

Fig. 6. An Illustration of the two conditions in our evaluation of EDBook. In CEDBook (left), participants performed a task with the EDBook platform. In CWeb+GPT (right), participants performed a task with equivalent content, converted to a webpage. CWeb+GPT participants can also interact with a “context-informed” instance of ChatGPT that has the context of the relevant webpage content to provide contextually-appropriate responses.

Figure 7. Counterbalanced study workflow. After screening, four groups of five participants each complete both EDBook and Web plus ChatGPT conditions, using Scheme and Cache tasks in opposite orders. The four sequences are EDBook Scheme then Web plus ChatGPT Cache; EDBook Cache then Web plus ChatGPT Scheme; Web plus ChatGPT Scheme then EDBook Cache; and Web plus ChatGPT Cache then EDBook Scheme. Each condition starts with up to 10 minutes of training, followed by up to 30 minutes on its task, up to 10 minutes of assessment, and up to 5 minutes of survey. All finish with an approximately 10-minute post-study interview.

Five pairs of box plots compare Web+GPT and EDBook: number of LLM questions, learning time, assessment time, assessment score, and attempts at example code. Mean values are respectively 3.45 versus 3.30 questions; 1389.90 versus 1817.85 seconds of learning; 575.0 versus 543.6 seconds of assessment; scores 1.35 versus 1.50; and 0.40 versus 0.95 example attempts. Learning time and example attempts differ significantly, as marked in Table 2.

Diverging bar charts compare the categories of questions asked in Web+GPT, blue bars to the left, and EDBook, pink bars to the right. Web+GPT has more requests to understand concepts, evaluate solutions, and directly create code. EDBook has more requests to apply concepts, analyze concepts, and converse outside a question.

Stacked five-category agreement bars compare Web+GPT and EDBook responses to the statements in Table 4. Colors run from strongly disagree in orange through neutral in gray to strongly agree in blue. EDBook receives more agreement for concept explanation, tutorial structure, engagement, and the usefulness of quiz questions. For EDBook-only features, 80 percent strongly agree code previews were useful, 55 percent strongly agree selecting among suggested messages was useful, and 50 percent strongly agree writing custom messages was useful.

Figure 8. EDBook data schema separates persistent page content from per-user state. Page data, stored as a JSON file, contains a target cell, a map of participants, a map of cells, and media files. Participants have an ID, name, color, and description. Each cell records its source, parent and child cells, sender, editor pointer decorations, file differences, and directives. Pointer decorations locate a filename and start and end line-column positions; differences represent added content, removed lines, or unchanged lines. User state, stored in browser local storage, contains the selected cell and a map of cell states. Each user-cell state records whether it has been passed and the states of its directives.

Figure 4.7 A preliminary version of InterState (then called Euclase). This version contains the basic object layout (states as columns and properties as rows). However, this version of Euclase does not differentiate between states and events. The state of an object is the last event that occurred on that object. Every object also has a draw field that specifies, in JavaScript canvas code, how it should be drawn (typically referencing other fields), as described in section 4.4.5. This example also utilizes the defunct KEEPVALUE primitive, described in section 4.4.1. Empty cell values are KEEP by default (greyed out in the figure); an idea that was maintained through the current version of InterState by replacing the “KEEP” keyword with a circle.

Early InterState state-machine design with trapezoidal state boxes. Transitions are drawn between points along the sloped lower edges, and event conditions are written on the connecting arrows. Adjacent state boxes consume substantial horizontal space.

Revised InterState state-machine layout. Compact rectangular state boxes sit above property columns. Transition arrows share the space above the states, reducing their horizontal footprint. The current state and active values are highlighted in green.

Breakout ball state machine with two main states, in_play and dead. Several collision events loop within in_play for the paddle, walls and blocks. A bottom collision ends play, and gameReset starts a new run. The many events around few states make this diagram wide, illustrating a layout limitation.

Figure 4.11 The InterState editor shows one object at a time (in this case, myShape) and the fields and current values of every parent object in the containment hierarchy (in this case, sketch and paper). The editor also allows developers to pin objects to the screen by dragging them to the bottom of the window.

Early Euclase editor using a tree of objects. Multiple expanded object tables and state machines are linked diagonally across the page, with highlighted property cells. The simultaneous display of parent and child objects creates the clutter that motivated the later one-object-at-a-time view.

InterState uses a prototype-instance inheritance model with multiple inheritance. Prototypes are simply specified in the prototypes property. Here, my_square inherits from square. Because my_square does not define a value for height, it inherits the definition of square.height, as indicated by the greyed out text in the columns on the right. Note that my_square inherits the definition of height, not the value. Thus, the width property of my_square evaluates to a different value (20) than the width of square (15).
An object that inherits from both draggable and selectable behaviors. Note that the definitions for the color property are inherited from draggable ('red') and selectable ('blue').

Figure 4.15 An object with multiple copies; copies is set to ['Jane', 'Sue']. Every copy has two properties: my_copy, which is set to that copy's item (here, either 'Jane' or 'Sue') and copy_num, which is set to that copy's index. Here, we are looking at the first copy (index 0).

Figure 4.16 Two InterState objects (favs_panel and color_disp) that create a dynamically changing display for a dynamic list of favorite colors. Annotations are in gold boxes. This code stores a list of favorites under favs_panel.favorites. When a user clicks on any color (represented favs_panel’s transition diagram as mouse.click(color), that color is added to the list of favorites (by setting favorites to favorites.push(color) in the color click transition). Because color_disp’s copies field is set to favorites, new copies of color_disp are added and removed as favorites changes, automatically adding and removing visual elements from the screen.
Figure 4.17 Syntax and runtime errors are highlighted in the editor but do not prevent the program from running. Fields with errors and other fields that depend on them are given the value undefined.

Task completion time, with means and standard-deviation error bars for 20 participants. Drag lock: JavaScript 19.3 minutes, SD 13.6; InterState 8.0 minutes, SD 6.8. Image carousel: JavaScript 28.3 minutes, SD 7.6; InterState 14.7 minutes, SD 5.5. InterState takes about half the time on both tasks; the surrounding text reports p less than .05 and p less than .01, respectively.

Three benchmark plots of update delay in milliseconds as object complexity grows. A gray band marks delays above 100 milliseconds as non-instantaneous. The yellow prototype-chain curve reaches this threshold at N equals 58; the blue number-of-prototypes curve at about 2,400; and the green number-of-children curve at about 1,200. Delay generally rises with complexity.

Figure 4.20 A representation of the basic object structure for the objects shown in Figure 4.13. The basic object tree is a mutable tree that gets modified when the developer performs an edit on their program. This model contains three objects (sketch, square, and my_square) and five cells (sq_protos, sq_width, sq_height, mysq_protos, and mysq_width). Note there is no field for my_square.height, the inherited field that only exists in the contextual object tree shown in Figure 4.21. There is also no slot for values, which are computed in the contextual object tree because the value of a given variable depends on its computation context. This model makes two simplifying assumptions. First, it omits the state machines of square and my_square (which would each have one start state). Second, it gives human-readable names to objects (sq_protos, sq_width, etc.) whereas in the InterState runtime, objects’ names only exist in their container object’s field name.

Contextual object tree corresponding to the basic tree above. The root contextual dictionary c_sketch has square and my_square children. Every contextual dictionary and cell references its underlying basic object and a context path, and cells additionally contain computed values. The inherited my_square.height exists here even though the basic my_square object defines no height cell. Changing a basic definition updates the contextual values that depend on it.

Figure 5.1 A state machine showing the various states of an event with priority p. Every event can be in three states: idle, pending fire, and pending block. By default, every event is in the idle state. When the event requests to fire (a), through the fire method, it enters the pending fire state. After enough time (specified by the timeout parameter) or if the event has no timeout parameter, then the event’s firing is confirmed (b). If the event firing is cancelled (through the cancel method) before the timeout interval passes, then the event is cancelled (c). If another event in the same group with higher priority is requested before the timeout interval passes, then the event moves to the pending block stage (g). If all of the events with a higher priority are cancelled, then the event will return to the pending fire state (f). If any other event with a higher priority fires, then the event is blocked (d). If another event is still pending fire when the event’s timeout interval passes, then the event is also blocked (e).

Figure 6.1 The default, “non-greedy” behavior for touch clusters is that every touch cluster can claim the same fingers. For instance, suppose a developer defines one three-finger touch cluster and three one-finger touch clusters across different elements in an interface. With non-greedy behavior, when the user presses three fingers down, all four touch cluster activation events would fire.

Figure 6.2 Like in Figure 6.1, here the developer has defined one three-finger touch cluster and three one-finger touch clusters. However, the developer has specified that the three-finger touch cluster should be “greedy”, so that other touch clusters should not fire with any of the touches used. In this case, when the user presses three fingers down, only the three-finger touch cluster will fire.

Figure 6.3 In most multi-touch devices, when a user taps a numeric input field, a numeric keypad is invoked. In this example, I augment that interaction to allow a user’s finger to also “nudge” the numeric slider left or right to select a number slightly lower or higher than the current value. Implemented with InterState’s touch extensions, this example uses path crossing events to determine if the user’s finger is moving horizontally or tapping the widget.

InterState numerical-slider definition with init, fingerDown, and slidingMode states. A touch starts tracking; crossEvent enters slidingMode. A timeout(100) self-transition repeatedly updates the numerical value during a sustained slide, and releasing the touch returns to init. Rows define the slider's position, offset, crossing event, value, and displayed value text.
Figure 6.4, initial drawing canvas: overlapping multicolored brush strokes appear on a white canvas, with the controls hidden below the screen.
Figure 6.4, one-finger gesture: swiping upward from the bottom of the drawing canvas reveals a panel of brush and pen choices.
Figure 6.4, two-finger gesture: swiping upward from the bottom of the drawing canvas reveals a panel of colored swatches for selecting the drawing color.

InterState oneFinger touch-event definition. numFingers is 1, downInside restricts the gesture's starting area, and delay is 100 milliseconds so a second finger can be detected before the one-finger event fires.

InterState twoFingers touch-event definition. numFingers is 2, greedy is true, and downInside restricts the gesture's starting area. The greedy two-finger event prevents both the one-finger and two-finger actions from firing together.

InterState brushesPanel definition. Its state machine contains hidden, dragging, and showing states, with tHide and tShow substates inside dragging. The oneFinger event controls dragging and release transitions. The x, y, width, and height constraint rows position the panel, make it follow the finger, and determine whether it remains docked or hides.

Figure 6.5 This example represents an undo/redo (or more generally, back/forward) mechanism for tablet applications. The user first presses down two fingers (in the diagram shown, the index and ring fingers) and presses a third to the left to undo or a third finger to the right to redo. To prevent conflicts with panning and scrolling gestures, this undo/redo gesture also cancels if the two finger centroid moves or scales past a low threshold.

Touch regions for the undo/redo gesture. Two central fingers establish an anchor. A dashed red rectangle extends to the left of that anchor and a dashed blue rectangle to the right. Pressing a third finger inside the left region requests undo; pressing inside the right region requests redo. The regions move relative to the two-finger touch cluster.
Dependency diagram with an arrow from x on the right to y on the left. The definition y equals x plus 1 makes y depend on x.
After x changes, the same dependency arrow points from x to y. The y node is colored red and explicitly labeled invalid, indicating that its cached value must be recomputed when requested.

documents.title: Implementing Multi-Touch Gestures with Touch Groups and Cross Events

assets.alt: Figure 1: An illustration of a two-finger swipe-right gesture implemented with touch groups and cross events. Touch groups summarize properties of groups of touch events that move in synchrony. Cross events fire when a touch group crosses a given path. In this gesture, a 'twoFin-gerRightSwipe' event fires after a two-finger touch group crosses a path 10 pixels to the right of where the touch group

Figure 2: A state machine showing the various states of a touch event with priority p. An event can be in three states: idle, pending fire, or pending block. By default, every event is in the idle state. When the event fires (a), it enters the pending state. After enough time (as defined by the timeout parameter, default:0), the event’s firing is confirmed (b). If the event firing is cancelled before the timeout interval passes, then the event is cancelled (c). If a higher priority event is requested before the timeout interval passes, then the event moves to the pending block stage (f). If any other event with a higher priority is confirmed, then the event is blocked (d). If all the events with a higher priority are cancelled, then the event will return to the pending fire state (g). If the event times out while in the “pending block” state, then the event is blocked (e) and does not fire.

Figure 3: The sequence of states for single-tap and double-tap gestures as a user performs a single-tap then a double-tap. The states and events that are shown here reference those that are defined in Figure 2. In this example, there are two instantiations of the state machine: one for single-tap and one for double-tap. The single-tap gesture uses timeout=dbl_interval and the double-tap gesture uses timeout=0. User actions are shown on the left. After the user performs a single tap, the single-tap event is requested and confirmed after dbl_interval milliseconds. When the user performs a double tap, the double-tap event blocks the single-tap event, because it has a higher priority.

Figure 4: The default, “non-greedy” behavior for touch groups is that every touch group can claim the same fingers. For instance, suppose a developer defines one three-finger touch group and three one-finger touch groups across different elements in an interface. With non-greedy behavior, when the user presses three fingers down, all four touch group activation events would fire.

Figure 5: Like in Figure 4, here the developer has defined one three-finger touch group and three one-finger touch groups. However, the developer has specified that the three-finger touch group should be “greedy”, so that other touch groups should not fire with any of the touches used. In this case, when the user presses three fingers down, only the three-finger touch group will fire.

Figure 6: Participants were given the code for a multi-touch behavior. In this example, the code implements a “tap” gesture. To gauge their understanding of the code, they were asked to select which behavior that code implemented, from the four choices at the bottom. Participants were given ten behaviors in one implementation (either touch* or touch groups/cross events) and then ten using the other implementation. We randomized the implemented behaviors, multiple choice options, and multiple-choice ordering.

Figure 7: The same (“tap”) behavior as Figure 6, implemented with cross events touch groups. In addition to being more concise than the touch* implementation of the same gesture, many modifications to this gesture that would require significant changes to the touch* implementation are straightforward. For example, changing this gesture from a one-finger tap to a two-finger tap requires significant changes to the touch* implementation but is a one-line change in the touch group/cross event implementation (updating the second line to numFingers: 2). Using correctness in this task as a measure of understanding, participants were better able to understand code written with touch groups and cross events than with touch* events.

Figure 8: An example of the UI for defining behaviors in the GUI / touch group + cross event condition via a state machine. The black dot symbolizes the start state. Small light squares symbolize states. The larger grey squares specify transition events (e.g., cross events or touch group events).

Figure 9: An illustration of a set of pressure-sensitive trackpad gestures. When the user presses three fingers on the trackpad, the selected window resizes in response (yellow, top right). When the user presses with two fingers, the viewport scrolls (blue, bottom left) or the window moves (red, bottom right) depending on the finger pressure. Our implementation manages conflicts between these three gestures and standard one-finger touches (grey, top left).

Figure 10: An illustration of three gestures for pressure-sensitive trackpads that manipulate text. Here, the user initiates “command mode” with a heavy (high pressure) one-finger press in the top left quadrant of the trackpad. As the user holds that finger down, they can perform a light (low pressure) one-finger vertical scroll gesture to select text (top), a heavy two-finger gesture to enumerate the selected text (middle), or a light two-finger scroll gesture to specify the selected text’s indentation (bottom). The paths that specify cross events that initiate the gesture are shown in red.

Figure 11: An illustration of HandMark menus. HandMark menus are contextual menus that a user invokes with a multi-finger gesture. We implemented two different version of hand-mark menus. In the two-finger version (left) the user invokes a context menu by pressing with two fingers. As the user moves their two fingers, the menu follows. The user can then use a third finger to select a single item. In the five-finger version (right), users invoke the context menu by pressing the touchscreen with five fingers. Menu items then follow the individual fingers as they move. Users can use a sixth finger to select a menu item.

Figure 12: An illustration of a custom contextual pie menu for touchscreen devices. We created three implementations with minimal changes to the gesture’s implementation: 1) the user holds their finger then selects a menu item, 2) the user taps their finger then selects a menu item, or 3) the user double taps their finger then selects a menu item.

documents.title: InterState: A Language and Environment for Expressing Interface Behavior

assets.alt: Figure 1: A basic InterState object, named draggable, which implements draggable and drag lock behaviors. Properties that control draggable’s display are represented as rows (e.g. x, y, and fill). States and transitions are represented as columns (e.g. no_drag and drag). An entry in a property’s row for a particular state specifies a constraint that controls that property’s value in that state. Here, while draggable is in the drag state, x and y will be constrained to mouse.x and mouse.y respectively, meaning draggable will follow the mouse.

Figure 3: InterState uses a prototype-instance inheritance model with multiple inheritance. Prototypes are simply specified in the prototypes property. Here, my_square inherits from square. Because my_square does not define a value for height, it inherits the definition of square.height, as indicated by the greyed out text in the columns on the right. Note that my_square inherits the definition of height, not the value. Thus, its width property evaluates to a different value (20) than it does in square (15).

Figure 4. InterState multiple inheritance combines selectable and draggable objects. Selectable has not_selected and selected states and supplies a blue fill when selected. Draggable has not_dragging and dragging states, supplies a red fill while dragging, and constrains x and y to mouse.x and mouse.y. The combined my_selectable_draggable object inherits both state machines and their property definitions; its prototypes field lists selectable before draggable.

Figure 5. InterState person_display object has copies ['Jane', 'Sue']. The selected first copy has my_copy 'Jane' and copy_num 0; the second has my_copy 'Sue' and copy_num 1. The copies control shows copy 1 of 2.

assets.alt: S equals the ordered sequence s sub 1, s sub 2, through s sub n. The summary S contains n sentences.
E equals the collection e sub 1, e sub 2, through e sub m. E contains m game events.
Basic classifier pipeline. A sentence s and the set of game events E enter a classifier. Its output F is the subset of E described by that sentence; F may be empty.

MLB.com Gameday screenshot used as the source of game events. It shows Boston playing Cleveland, with a central batter-and-pitch display and pitch trajectories, the score and inning across the top, player and field information at left, a line score and batting statistics at right, and a play-by-play panel below. The application exposes pitch speed, movement and outcome along with game statistics.

Screenshot of an unassembled inning XML file. Nested inning, top or bottom half, at-bat and pitch elements store the play-by-play data. Attributes identify the batter, pitcher, balls, strikes, outs and a natural-language play description. Appendix A supplies a native-text example of the combined XML representation.

Screenshot of an unassembled players XML file. Player elements are grouped by away and home team; attributes provide identifiers and names plus game statistics. The system uses these player records to interpret names in summaries. Appendix A provides a native-text sample of the assembled player records.

Boston-perspective newspaper-style game summary, shown as an example of natural-language training text. It describes the same Boston–Cleveland game as the adjacent Cleveland summary; the two summaries select and emphasize different events.

Cleveland-perspective game summary for the same game as the adjacent Boston summary. The differing narrative perspective illustrates why one game can supply several distinct natural-language summaries.

Weka Explorer classifier output. The Classify tab displays the learned J48 decision tree, with indented branches for feature tests and leaf predictions, followed by evaluation statistics and a confusion matrix. Controls at left select the classifier and testing method. This is an example of the tree learned from sentence–event feature pairs; it is not a separate algorithm specification.

One-stage classification pipeline. The sentence and event set are expanded into sentence–event pairs. Simple and generated features are extracted for each pair, and a C4.5 classifier decides whether the event belongs in the set described by the sentence. All candidate pairs, including null events, go through this classifier.

Two-stage classification pipeline. A first feature extractor and C4.5 classifier decide whether the sentence discusses any game event. If its discussed-event set is empty, the output is the empty set. Otherwise the sentence is paired with candidate events, a second feature extractor and classifier evaluate those pairs, and the accepted events form F, the subset of E described by the sentence.
P of w-e given w-f equals P of w-e times P of w-f given w-e, divided by P of w-f; proportional to P of w-e times P of w-f given w-e.
Sentence–event score is proportional to P of e times P of s given e.

Translation-like classification pipeline. Each sentence is paired with candidate events. An element-probability model computes P(e), and a sentence-for-element model computes P(s given e). Their product ranks events. A separate result-size predictor, informed by sentence position and part-of-speech analysis, chooses how many highest-ranked events form the final subset F.
Approximate probability of event e: count of events with the same type as e that are discussed by some sentence, divided by count of all events with the same type as e.
Smoothed event probability: one plus the count of discussed events of the same type as e, divided by count of all events of that type plus the number of possible event types.

Named-entity recognition examples. Player mentions such as Gary Sheffield, Chien-Ming Wang, Webb and Johnson are highlighted and labeled Player. New York is marked as a Location and Red Sox as a Team. The labels distinguish entities from the surrounding sentence text.

Game-summary excerpt illustrating inning inference. The first sentence says Johnson came out dealing in the first inning; the following sentence describes his first pitch, an ensuing strikeout and fly outs. The later events inherit the inning context established by the earlier sentence.

Score sub s,e equals v-pitcher times rho-pitcher, plus v-batter times rho-batter, plus v-other-players times rho-other-players, plus v-stems times rho-stems, plus v-inning-match times rho-inning-match. Each rho is a learned multiplier for the corresponding feature.
P of s given e equals score sub s,e divided by the sum, over all sentences s-i, of score sub s-i,e.

Scatter plot of normalized sentence location from 0 to 1 against the number of game events discussed. Most points lie at zero or one event, fewer at two, and isolated points reach three to six. Sentences in the middle and later part of a summary more often discuss events than opening sentences.

Stacked area chart of predicted sentence context across normalized summary position. The blue Game Events share rises from about one tenth near the beginning to a peak near two fifths around 65 percent of the way through, then declines toward the end. The red Other share fills the remainder. The shape is the fitted context estimate used by the result-size predictor.

Two baseball sentences annotated with part-of-speech and entity tags. Player names and Red Sox are assigned PLAYER and TEAM labels; other words retain grammatical tags such as IN, CD, NN, VBD, AT and TO. The first example begins With two outs, Jay Payton produced an RBI single. These annotations supply the verb-related features for estimating how many events a sentence describes.

Horizontal frequency chart of errors in estimating the number of discussed events. Zero error dominates at roughly 420 cases. Errors of plus or minus one occur much less often, and errors with larger magnitude are rare. The chart supports the surrounding statement that estimating result size remains a bottleneck.

Figure 1: Editing conflicts in real-time collaborative notebooks can be implicit. As shown on the left, one can get an unexpected execution result because the collaborator accidentally changed the shared variable. As shown on the right, PADLOCK helps data scientists resolve editing conflicts in real-time collaborative editing in computational notebooks.

Figure 2: Overview of the three conflict-free mechanisms in PADLOCK. (A) Cell-level access control allows collaborators to claim ownership of the code cells and restrict others from editing or viewing them: (A1) Unchecking edit access for a user will change the cell background and disable editing; (A2) Unchecking read access for a user will blur the cell. (B) Variable-level access control extends the idea of access control from cells to shared variables: (B1) Unchecking a user’s variable access; (B2) After losing access, they will not be able to edit the variable and will receive warning when attempting to do so. (C) Parallel cell groups define a designated area where changes of the code and runtime state stay inside its own scope: (C1) One parallel cell group can contain multiple tabs; (C2) Each tab can contain multiple cells; (C3) Sync the variables from the global scope to the current active tab; (C4) Add a new tab; (C5) Click the radio button to mark it as the “main” tab.

assets.alt: Figure 1. VRCopilot offers three creation modes. Automatic creation generates an entire furnished room from a voice request. Manual creation combines pointing and speech to request a chair at a location, then offers three candidate chairs for selection. Scaffolded creation lets the user draw or generate labeled floor-plan wireframes, such as a bed footprint, and convert them into furniture.

Figure 2 shows the user interfaces in VRCopilot including (a) a palette menu where users can select and furniture from the catalog, and (b) a multi-workspace visualization that allows users to work and switch between multiple versions.

Figure 3. Three five-step workflows for furnishing a bedroom. Manual creation: request a bed at a pointed location, choose a suggested bed, request a nightstand, choose it, and place it beside the bed. Automatic creation: request room furniture, review a generated room, delete an unwanted item, inspect the reduced layout, then add or adjust furniture. Scaffolded creation: generate floor-plan wireframes, label a selected region as a bed, turn labeled wireframes into furniture, adjust the arrangement, and retain the completed room.

Figure 4. System architecture. A Unity client coordinates direct manipulation, voice requests and intents, intermediate wireframe representations, and the 3D scene. Audio is sent to OpenAI whisper-1, whose transcript is processed by gpt-4-turbo to return intents and parameters to Unity. The client requests layouts from the ATISS generative model server, receives generated wireframe layouts, and instantiates furniture in the scene. AWS Polly provides text-to-speech audio output. Users can also directly manipulate the scene and draw wireframes through the client interface.

Figure 5a. Top-down apartment layout created by P7 without generative AI. Two furnished bedrooms sit above an open living and kitchen area. The lower area has seating along the bottom edge and a broad open center; bedroom furniture includes additional storage or work surfaces.

Figure 5b. Top-down apartment layout created by P10 without generative AI. Two bedrooms appear above a living and dining area with an L-shaped sofa on the left and a rectangular dining table and chairs in the center. The bedrooms use a coordinated pale furniture palette.

Figure 5c. P6 used generative AI for the two bedrooms and created the remainder of the apartment without AI. Both upper bedrooms are densely furnished. The lower living area contains a sofa and two round tables with a broad open space to the right.

Figure 5d. P13 used generative AI for all rooms. The two upper bedrooms and lower living area have varied furniture. In the lower area, a sofa and round table are at left, a long dining table occupies the center-right, and a desk sits diagonally near the bottom-left corner.

Figure 6. Box plots of agency, creativity, and effort on a seven-point Likert scale, comparing manual creation in red, scaffolded creation in green, and automatic creation in blue. Manual creation has the highest agency ratings, scaffolded creation is intermediate, and automatic creation is lowest; all pairwise agency differences are significant. Manual creation also has higher creativity ratings than the other two conditions, which do not significantly differ. Effort ratings cluster near the lower-middle of the scale and do not significantly differ. Boxes show the middle half of responses with median lines, whiskers, and plotted means.

Mini avatars are anchored in the history graph that represents which version users are in. Users can also create a portal to monitor another user’s first-person view. A shared history visualization facilitates group discussion by anchoring the HG to a shared location in the virtual scene and allowing users to discuss and to preview a version and reuse objects collaboratively.

Inside the menu, there are six sub-menus of pre-made furniture models: sofas, tables, chairs, desks, storage, and lights. On top of the history graph it shows how V4 to V8 expand as part of the DAG, where each operation will generate a new node in the DAG. At the bottom it shows a new branch that only shows the version that another collaborator is in.

Figure 4.a: A screenshot of the history graph that contains three branches in the system. Each branch is represented by different colors of edges between the nodes including light green, red, and dark green. The user is currently on the branch colored in light green.
Figure 4.b: A screenshot of the history graph after the user switches the branch and now they are selecting the branch colored in red.

The preview is labeled as “V5.11_preview”. Figure 5.b: A screenshot of reusing objects in the preview. The user is in V14 and they are viewing a preview of V5.11. Figure 1. Four panels compare simulated and human cursor motion through sine-wave and square-wave tunnels. Orange simulated speed repeatedly rises and falls in the sine tunnel, broadly matching the blue human speed trend. In the square tunnel, the blue human speed has higher, sharper peaks while simulated speed is lower and smoother. Both simulated and human trajectories follow the tunnel shapes; the square-turn paths round the corners. Shaded bands show variability.

Figure 2. Three cascading-menu examples compare human and simulated cursor trajectories from a green starting point to a red target in a submenu. The highlighted orange and blue paths bend diagonally between the menus; the submenu target height increases across the examples. Both path sets show similar curved routes through the menu corridor.

Figure 3. Three icon-grid examples show lasso selection of green target icons among gray distractors. Highlighted human and simulated paths loop around the target clusters while avoiding neighboring icons. The paths bend around different target shapes and remain close to the target boundaries.
